previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted with malaise, productive cough with yellowish-green sputum, shortness of breath, and left ear pain. Initial chest X-ray showed no acute infiltrates, but CT chest revealed bronchial thickening and centrilobular nodules consistent with active infection. He was started on IV Vancomycin and Zosyn for suspected pneumonia, later transitioned to oral levofloxacin. ENT confirmed otitis media, treated with otic drops. His acute kidney injury, likely prerenal from volume depletion, resolved with IV fluids. Coumadin was restarted for atrial fibrillation. He improved clinically, remained afebrile, and was discharged home on oral antibiotics, with plans to initiate Revlimid for multiple myeloma and follow up with ENT and anticoagulation clinic.

somnolence and states that it is due to his lack of sleep over 
the last few days. His dyspnea is improved, but not resolved. He 
is no longer coughing. He has no other complaints.

IMPRESSION:

Brief Hospital Course:
# ACUTE RENAL FAILURE: Patient presented in ARF with Cr of 4.7 
from 1.2 10 days prior. This was thought to be due to a 
combination of multiple myeloma progression and hypercalcemia 
causing pre-renal ARF. Renal U/S negative for obstruction and 
FENa was 1.1%. He was treated with IVF for his ARF as well as 
his hypercalcemia (see below) and his renal function improved. 
He was seen by nephrology who agreed with management. His Cr was 
1.1 on the day of discharge. 
.
# HYPERCALCEMIA/HYPOCALCEMIA: Patient presented with Ca of 15. 
His only symptom was shortness of breath when he presented to 
the ED. On admission he was treated with aggressive IV 
hydration, calcitonin, steroids and pamidronate (90mg once). His 
Ca level returned to ___ after 2 days and calcitonin was 
stopped. Subsequently his Ca level continued to decrease and he 
met the criteria for hypocalcemia. Again he was asymptomatic. He 
was treated with aggressive calcium repletion, both IV and PO, 
and vitamin D. He had persistent hypocalcemia thereafter 
requiring aggressive repletion. This was thought to be due to 
pamidronate. This medication was given when the patient was in 
ARF, he was given the max dose and it probably was not being 
excreted at the normal rate so it caused hypocalcemia. His PTH 
was found to be high while patient had hypocalcemia. This was 
thought to be a reaction to hypocalcemia, not a primary 
parathyroid problem. PTHrp was pending upon discharge and should 
be followed up. Upon discharge his corrected Ca level was 7.2, 
he was continued on oral Ca repletion, vitamin D and had follow 
up appointments for Ca checks the day after discharge and the 
day after.
.
# ELEVATED INR: Patient presented with an INR of 16. The 
etiology of this was unclear but it was thought to be due to 
decreased PO intake causing vitamin K depletion and the patient 
taking too much coumadin as an outpatient. On presentation he 
received FFP, vitamin K and his coumadin was stopped. His INR 
continued to trend down and when   it returned to ___ and his 
ARF had resolved he was restarted on coumadin. Initially at 5mg 
daily and on discharge he was continued on his outpatient 
regimen. 
.
# MULTIPLE MYELOMA: Patient's presentation was concerning for 
disease progression, given that it was known that his disease 
had relapsed. Patient's treatment with revlemid was stopped on 
admission given his ARF. Once his renal function was improving 
his revelemid was re-started at 5mg ___ of home dose) on ___. 
Once his renal function was back to ___ his dose was increased 
to 10mg. His MM markers were found to have improved since last 
assessment. He was instructed to take revlemid 10mg for 3 days 
after discharge to complete his 28 day cycle.
.
# DYSPNEA: Initial concern was for infection (viral vs 
bacterial) although patient had had no fevers or any other 
localizing symptoms. Given his recent admission for pneumonia he 
was treated for HAP with vancomycin/cefepime (7 day course) and 
for CAP with azithromycin (4 day course). He also received 
standing nebulizer treatments for his COPD as this could have 
contributed to his presentation.
.
# AFIB: Patient had a history of atrial fibrillation. His HR 
remained in the ___ range. His coumadin was restarted prior 
to discharge and his INR was 1.8 at the time.
.
# CAD s/p MI: Patient asx and currently NS bradycardia. His 
metoprolol was held due to his persistent bradycardia and his 
aspirin stopped due to elevated INR. The patient was instructed 
to re-start his metoprolol as an outpatient. Patient was 
instructed not to continue treatment with aspirin as he was 
already being anticoagulated with coumadin.
.
# DEPRESSION: Continued outpatient citalopram.

Activity Status:Ambulatory - Independent

 
Discharge Instructions:
You were admitted to because you were having shortness of breath 
at home. Upon admission you were found to have an elevated 
calcium level in the blood, an elevated INR (coumadin number) 
and acute kidney failure. We treated you with IV fluids and 
medications to lower your calcium and this resolved. We treated 
your kidney failure with IV fluids and your kidney function 
returned to normal levels. We treated your elevated INR with 
transfusions of plasma and vitamin K administration and this 
decreased to normal levels. We re-started your coumadin on the 
day before your discharge. We treated your shortness of breath 
with antibiotics, this resolved and the antibiotics were 
stopped. Your calcium was then found to be low and you needed 
daily calcium repletion. You also had bacteria in your urine and 
were given antibiotics for this.

You will need to come back to the clinic for blood tests on ___ 
and ___

Medication Changes:
STOP: Aspirin 81 mg daily
START: Calcium Carbonate 500mg three times a day
START: Vitamin D 800 units daily
No other changes made   
 
Followup Instructions:
___

radiology_notes.text:
PORTABLE CHEST RADIOGRAPH PERFORMED ON ___

Comparison is made with a prior CT chest from ___ as well as a chest
radiograph from ___.

CLINICAL HISTORY:  Shortness of breath, multiple myeloma, recent chemotherapy
and recent pneumonia.  Question pneumonia.

FINDINGS:  AP upright portable chest radiograph was obtained.  Compared with
the prior radiograph and chest CT, there appears to be resolution of
previously noted opacities in the right upper lung, though given the
relatively radiographically occult nature of these findings on prior chest
radiographs, persistent residual infection cannot be entirely excluded.  No
large pleural effusions are seen, though the CP angles are partially excluded.
Cardiomediastinal silhouette is normal.  There is no evidence of congestive
heart failure.  Deformity at the right distal clavicle is stable.

IMPRESSION:  No definite signs of infection though given the subtlely of prior
CT findings, persistent minimal infection cannot be entirely excluded.

HISTORY:  A ___ man with creatinine of 4.6 acutely.  Evaluate for
vascular thrombosis.

RENAL ULTRASOUND WITH DOPPLERS.

COMPARISON:  CTA pelvis ___.

FINDINGS:  The bladder is decompressed with a Foley, and has an irregular 
contour, consistent with history of reconstruction.  There is slight cortical
scarring and atrophy of the left upper pole, but no stones or hydronephrosis. 
The right kidney is normal in echotexture without stones, masses, or
hydronephrosis.  The right kidney measures 11.6 cm and the left kidney
measures 10.9 cm.  Color and pulsed Doppler assessment of the renal
vascularity is limited by excessive patient motion, but there is gross patency
of right and left renal arteries and veins with grossly normal
normal-appearing waveforms. There is no fluid identified in the abdomen or
pelvis.

IMPRESSION:  No renal stones or hydronephrosis.   Reconstructed bladder. 
Gross patency of bilateral renal arteries and veins.  Probable scarring of
left kidney, unchanged.

CT CHEST WITHOUT CONTRAST, ___

INDICATION:  MM recent recurrence, now with dyspnea and cough.  Question of
intrathoracic process.

COMPARISON:  ___ and multiple priors.

TECHNIQUE:  Volumetric CT of the chest performed without contrast per
departmental protocol including multiplanar reformations.

FINDINGS:  Diffuse bilateral bronchiolitis has now improved.  Previously noted
centrilobular nodules, ground-glass opacity, and linear branching opacities
have nearly completely resolved, except in the scattered areas of the
bilateral upper lobes and in the lingula.  Moderately severe bronchial wall
thickening is not significantly changed, though areas of mucoid impaction are
slightly improved, particularly at the lung bases.  Right basilar atelectasis
is also improved.

Scattered mediastinal lymph nodes again do not meet CT criteria for pathologic
enlargement, measuring up to 7 mm in short axis in the paratracheal region. 
Central airways are patent to the subsegmental level.  Heart size remains
normal.  There is no pleural or pericardial effusion.  Moderate coronary
artery calcifications are unchanged.

This study is not specifically tailored for subdiaphragmatic evaluation. 
Within the partially imaged upper abdomen, note is made of gas within the left
renal collecting system, of uncertain etiology.

There is no osseous lesion suspicious for malignancy.  Right clavicular
deformity related to prior fracture is stable.  Slight compression deformity
of a mid thoracic vertebral body is new since previous CT of ___.

IMPRESSION:

1.  Improved bronchiolitis, with near complete resolution of centrilobular
nodules and ground-glass opacity.  Residual bronchial airway thickening
remains moderate.

2.  New slight compression deformity of a mid thoracic spine vertebral body,
probably T7.

3.  Gas in the left renal collecting system, of uncertain etiology.  This may
be related to the patient's neobladder, or recent catheterization, especially
if there is ureteral reflux (left ureter is noted to have been dilated on
previous imaging studies).  Clinical correlation recommended to exclude
gas-forming infection, e.g. emphysematous pyelitis.

Initial findings discussed with Dr. ___ on ___.  Final
report discussed with Dr. ___ at 10:20 on ___.
